national.title: U.S. adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist after Nvidia scandal
national.summary: The Trump administration restricted Megaspeed from buying advanced semiconductor chips, after the firm's alleged links to China helped kick-start the scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
national.body: The Trump administration on Monday restricted Singapore-based Megaspeed from buying advanced semiconductor chips, after the firm's alleged links to China helped kick-start the scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. An operator of data centers in Southeast Asia, Megaspeed has been accused of transferring the high-tech Nvidia chips that power artificial intelligence to China, which the company denies. Huang also admitted earlier this month to having an affair with a former Megaspeed executive who U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese intelligence asset.The U.S. Commerce Department added Megaspeed to the Entity List, a designation that prevents it from buying sensitive U.S. technologies — including advanced chips — without a license from the federal government.Megaspeed has already been on Nvidia's internal "no sell" list since June 2025, the Justice Department and Commerce Department said in a joint statement last week.CBS News has reached out to Megaspeed for comment.The crackdown on Megaspeed came just hours after Nvidia's fortunes dramatically turned around — partly at the Trump administration's behest.The semiconductor giant's board of directors reinstated Huang as CEO early Monday, less than two weeks after Huang resigned following allegations of extramarital affairs with the Megaspeed executive and a subordinate at Nvidia. President Trump told CNBC he personally spoke with Nvidia's board and "convinced them" to rehire Huang, giving the board "assurances" on national security. Nvidia's share price leaped more than 30% after the decision.

national.title: Federal appeals court gives President Donald Trump a path to erasing hush money conviction
national.summary: The decision moves the case to a federal court, where Trump could seek to have charges dismissed on immunity grounds.
national.body:
Michael Sisak, Associated Press Michael Sisak, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — A federal appeals court on Monday gave President Donald Trump a new pathway to erasing his hush money criminal conviction, moving the case to a federal court where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds.

A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a lower court decision that had kept the case in state court in New York, where Trump was tried and convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The panel ordered a lower court to promptly issue a decision on whether the case should remain in federal court. If that happens, Trump could then argue that verdict should be discarded because of presidential immunity.

The decision also set in motion a halt to proceedings in Trump's simultaneous state court appeal. Trump denies wrongdoing and was given no punishment in the case, which made him the first U.S. president convicted of a crime.

In a two-page order, the 2nd Circuit panel said it disagreed with the late U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein's earlier denial of Trump's request to move the historic case from state court to federal court, a process known as removal.

The appellate judges ruled that Hellerstein "erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case" after a conviction and erred in denying that Trump had good cause to make two attempts at moving the case — once after his indictment and again after his trial.

national.title: California Democrat to resign from Congress after evidence of sexual misconduct
national.summary: Jimmy Gomez, who lost his election this month and only serving in the House until the year's end, was accused of sexual misconduct with a staff member.
national.body:
California Representative Jimmy Gomez has said he will resign from Congress after an investigation found credible evidence that he engaged in sexual misconduct, according to CBS News.

A report released on Monday by the House Ethics Committee stated that Gomez, a Los Angeles Democrat, made "unwelcome sexual advances" toward a House staff member, "disregarding the power imbalance inherent" between them.

Gomez, 51, said he disagreed with the report findings but he would resign on 1 Dec. He lost his seat in the midterm elections earlier this month and is only serving in the House of Representatives until the end of the year.

national.summary: The U.S. Army plans to detonate 68 drums of lead azide in Iowa despite local leaders and residents raising concerns.
national.body: The U.S. Army's plan to detonate several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa has been delayed multiple times amid a court battle and community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume for miles.The Army said the controlled detonation of lead azide is necessary due to the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own."Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the Army said in a statement. President Trump said Monday, without the demolition, "a very dangerous situation exists," but ordered the Army to halt the plan, deferring to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit and Iowa's Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand.So why exactly does the Army need to detonate the chemicals and what are the risks to the public?Why does the Army need to detonate lead azide in Iowa?In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.Lead azide is a highly sensitive primary initiating explosive. Due to its extreme sensitivity, even minor external triggers, such as sparks, open flames, friction or pinpricks, can detonate it.The recrystallization of lead azide can have a high risk of spontaneous explosion, which the EPA said creates a highly unstable and dangerous situation.Additionally, cold weather would further destabilize the explosive materials. national.title: Jimmy Gomez to resign after Ethics panel finds evidence of misconduct
national.summary: The bipartisan committee said Rep. Jimmy Gomez made unwanted sexual advances and sexual contact with a House staffer.
national.body: Washington — Rep. Jimmy Gomez announced Monday that he will resign from Congress, with the announcement coming shortly after the House Ethics Committee released a report saying it found "substantial evidence" that the California Democrat engaged in sexual misconduct, including making unwanted sexual advances and sexual contact with a House staffer. Gomez said he had "strong disagreements" with the findings, but saw "no other alternative than to resign." He said his resignation is effective Dec. 1 "to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs." "I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee's report and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage," Gomez said in a statement. Gomez was set to leave office in early January after losing his reelection bid. The bipartisan committee announced in August that it was looking into the allegations. As part of its investigation, the panel interviewed one woman who said Gomez made unwanted sexual advances toward her while she was a House staffer on two occasions, including one in which he made "sexual contact" with her in public and another where she described him as "forceful" with her in his congressional office, according to the report. "Representative Gomez failed in his obligation to behave in a manner that reflects creditably on the House, and his conduct was exacerbated by his failure to appreciate the inherent power imbalance between House Members and House staff," the report said. The report said Gomez's conduct caused the woman "significant and ongoing distress" and contributed to her decision to leave her job. This is a breaking story; check back for updates.

national.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
national.summary: Ukraine's sinking of a Russian battleship at a port in Libya raises the stakes of the war a notch, writes Frank Gardner.
national.body:
Anchored up in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi , co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?

The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.

Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes , has called it "a dangerous escalation".

It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.

Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

national.summary: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House.
national.body: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on election night as the GOP was on track to lose many of the districts it tried to gerrymander last year. There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP. But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House and are on track to win at least 258 House seats, flipping dozens of GOP-held districts.With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party. national.summary: According to a recent survey, about 63% of Americans are using credit cards to buy increasingly expensive groceries – and many are having trouble paying off that food debt.
national.body: Those beeps at the checkout counter aren't music to anyone's ears these days. Each one is an ear-piercing reminder of how just much more we're paying for groceries this Thanksgiving – 32% more, to be exact – than we paid in 2020, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. One mother shopping with her daughter told us, "Feels like all my money goes to food."The USDA doesn't report food insecurity figures like they used to; that survey was discontinued last year. What we do know is, in 2024 nearly 14% of Americans said they were struggling to eat, making this Thanksgiving yet another exercise in the art of the possible.First, consumers are changing where we shop. Discount grocery chains like Aldi, Lidl, and Food 4 Less are reporting greater and greater market shares, giving traditional supermarkets, like Kroger, a real run for their money. David Rinaldo, chief operating officer at Aldi, says there used to be a stigma around discount stores. Now, Aldi is on track to open 150 stores this year alone. "I never would have dreamed we'd ever get to the point that it would be that mainstream, that people would come to a limited assortment discount grocer to be where they shop," Rinaldo said. Part of the draw? Cheaper in-house brands, contracted out to manufacturers that make them for stores like Aldi and others – assembly lines tailored to a specific market. They aren't the no-name generic brands you might remember from the 1970s and '80's. These are different. It's what fills 92% of what's on Aldi's shelves. Private labels, says Rinaldo, aren't the exception; they're now the trend. "I think there's been a movement with private label," he said. "Nine out of the last ten years, private label has grown faster than national brands."But it's not just where American are buying groceries; it's how they're paying for them that is changing. According to a recent survey by the Urban Institute in Washington, D.C., about 63% of us are using credit cards to buy groceries. national.title: Trump orders US military not to detonate toxic explosives in Iowa without court approval
national.summary: The US Army had said it planned to detonate the explosives on Wednesday despite a court-ordered pausea as public outcry intensified.
national.body:
President Donald Trump said he has ordered the US army not to move ahead with plans to detonate five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa on Wednesday until a court rules on the issue.

The administration previously had planned to go forward with the plans despite legal challenges and public outcry over the potential health risks to nearby communities.

A court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation.

"I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward," Trump said, referencing the court that halted the detonation.

He added in his post on Truth Social that the US had "an opportunity to do a highly controlled detonation of these dangerous and rapidly corroding materials" because of optimal weather.

Even after the court pause ordered on Thursday, the justice department told the court that the army intends to move forward with its plan, because of an "immediate risk" that those materials could "spontaneously explode".

Environmental groups have accused the government of skirting the judicial process.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.

national.title: Airline glitches and storms could make Thanksgiving travel messy
national.summary: A cascade of technical glitches that have upended airlines over the past week are adding to the unease.
national.body:
Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past weeks, the threat of storms on both coasts and soaring airfares.

No wonder Americans are feeling jittery going into the busiest travel week of the year.

On top of all that, there's concern that a big storm brewing along the East Coast could ground the big balloons in the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

The biggest unknown for travelers is whether airlines will be upended again by new system failures.

First there was the Federal Aviation Administration's network malfunction setting off the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. Then last week, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines saw their own outages, leading to hundreds of flight delays.

"You do your best to be patient, but it's also helpful to have some context of what's going on, because our lives are literally in your hands," said Chianti Blackmon, a college administrator who was at the Atlanta airport on Monday.

Delta said that its operations were stable Monday, a day after over 1,000 of its flights were delayed after an automated system that calculates aircraft weight malfunctioned.

"Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers," the airline said.

national.title: Trump says Army will not detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa without court approval
national.summary: President Donald Trump says he will defer to a federal appeals court on whether to proceed with detonating degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant.
national.body:
Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press

President Donald Trump on Monday said he will defer to a federal appeals court on whether the administration moves ahead with plans to detonate several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant.

The detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide was initially planned for Friday, but the Army has since changed the date three times following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. They had planned for a detonation on Wednesday, saying the weather was most favorable that day.

The Army had no immediate comment when asked about the president's social media post. Environmentalists sued last week in an effort to stop the detonation, winning a stay from the appeals court pending a decision on the validity of an emergency permit approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency that cleared the way for the operation. Trump said he prefers to take care of the volatile material as soon as possible and that a controlled detonation would be much safer. "At the same time, have ordered the military not to do so until such time as the 8th Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing to the operation," Trump said in a statement. If Sand and the court don't agree, Trump said the administration will have no choice but to not proceed with the planned detonation, adding that he would hold the incoming governor responsible for "any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation."

Sand said in a social media post on Sunday that because of previous decisions that have already been made, "No good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been."

He questioned why a contract to remove the explosive risk was canceled, why nothing was done and "why we are rushing to demolition now in late November."

"The safety of Iowans should be the top priority of everyone involved," he said. "All relevant federal, state and local government resources should be focused on protecting everyone that could be impacted."

Some residents near Middletown, where the ammunition plant is located, have been sealing their windows and doors as a precaution to keep out any lead dust that might result from the detonation. Others who live farther away were raising concern on social media about the possible paths that the plume could take depending on shifts in the wind.

national.title: Senate leadership vote tests newly elected Democrats' promise of change
national.summary: The Democratic Party's incoming senators face an early test of their campaign promises to shake up Washington as they decide who will lead their new majority.
national.body:
Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Democratic Party's incoming senators haven't even been sworn into office yet, but the decision over who will lead their new majority is already testing the promise of change they made as candidates.

The 13 new Democrats are part of the largest incoming Senate class in decades, with several winning in Republican strongholds by promising to shake up Washington and be independent voices. Now they are caught up in a classic insider fight, forced to decide whether to stick with longtime Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York or back challenger Chris Van Hollen of Maryland.

Newly elected progressives, including Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, have backed Van Hollen, who is taking on Schumer with promises of a more aggressive legislative approach. Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio, who is returning to Washington after losing his seat in 2024, supports Schumer.

But the incoming senators from traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Mississippi, Iowa and South Carolina, whose victories helped deliver Democrats the majority, have so far largely avoided taking sides publicly. Annie Andrews of South Carolina has said she is talking with both candidates. Scott Colom of Mississippi says he wants to get to know them better before deciding and describes himself as being in "listening mode."

Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said Thursday he would not back Schumer, but declined to endorse anyone.

"I'm looking for someone who is going to bring people together," Hamilton told MSNow. "Right now, in places like Kansas, there's a lot of people who don't feel that in Chuck Schumer."

Schumer's long-standing relationships and knowledge of Senate machinery are a big advantage heading into the Dec. 1 vote, which will be held by secret ballot. He also oversees Senate Democrats' campaign spending group, funneling millions into many of the races and, in some cases, recruiting the candidates to run in the first place.

national.title: Trump says he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
national.summary: The US president personally intervened to speak to members of Nvidia's board of directors.
national.body:
President Donald Trump said he spoke to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.

In a brief interview with CNBC, Trump said that he gave the board "assurances" that Huang's extramarital affair did not present a national security issue for the US.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of a series of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.

The US president, however, has repeatedly expressed support for the embattled CEO despite the vocal opposition of lawmakers - including some Republicans - to his being reinstated at the company.

"I spoke to them [the board], let me put it that way," Trump told CNBC. "And I convinced them."

Additionally, Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating Huang.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is set to condemn California Gov. Gavin Newsom's clemency to the state's death row inmates in a speech at the Justice Department on Monday, his second address in less than two years at an agency that has moved aggressively to fulfill his White House's agenda and pursue criminal cases against his adversaries.

The White House said the speech, in the building's ceremonial Great Hall, would be about protecting American families and Newsom's decision to commute the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to punishments of life without parole.

But it was unclear to what extent the address would also function as a forum for the Republican president to again encourage the prosecution of his political opponents and revisit years-old grievances about a Justice Department that has repeatedly investigated him over the past decade.

national.title: Writers unhappy with PEN America's response to war in Gaza form new chapter
national.summary: Novelist Maaza Mengiste says they don't seek rivalry with PEN America but differ in structure and priorities.
national.body:
Hillel Italie, Associated Press Hillel Italie, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — Ta-Nehisi Coates, M. Gessen and Jacqueline Woodson are among more than 100 writers, editors, agents and others in the literary community seeking to establish a chapter of PEN that is independent from PEN America, the longtime free expression organization that has endured tensions with various members in recent years over the war in Gaza and other issues.

The new group, called PEN Writes US, would be "guided by the PEN Charter's vision of 'one humanity, living in peace and equality in one world,'" Monday's announcement by the proposed organization reads.

Novelist Maaza Mengiste told The Associated Press during a recent telephone interview that PEN Writes does not seek to be a rival of PEN America and will likely share common ground about fighting censorship and oppression and encouraging discussions among writers. But she did say that PEN Writes will differ in its structure and in some of its priorities, ideally becoming "a center where sustained and equal advocacy for all writers guides principles, rather than institutional caution."

Numerous writers and activists have been unhappy with PEN America's response to the war in Gaza, contending that PEN America has been reluctant to criticize Israel or to defend the rights of Palestinian writers with the same force it has advocated for writers elsewhere.

"I think there's been a feeling for quite a while that PEN's response to the war in Gaza has been inadequate," says PEN Writes member Francine Prose, a former president of PEN America.

Fallout from the war in Gaza led PEN America to call off its annual awards show and "World Voices" festival in 2024 because so many participants dropped out. (Those events resumed in 2025 and 2026). Last summer, PEN America President Dinaw Mengestu resigned after PEN published a report about obstacles and harassment faced by Israeli and Jewish writers since the war began in 2023.

Mengestu, a prize-winning novelist who is now a member of PEN Writes, at the time cited the report's criticism of cultural boycotts and expressed support for the Palestinian-led boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, or BDS. Organizers advocate economic and cultural pressure on Israel to end the country's occupation of territories captured in the 1967 Mideast war, grant full equality to Arab citizens of Israel and promote the rights of Palestinian refugees to return.

national.title: Some sheriffs who signed pacts to help Trump's immigration enforcement efforts ousted by voters
national.summary: Trump has encouraged local law enforcement agencies to sign partnerships with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. More than 2,700 agreements are in place nationwide.
national.body:
Sarah Rankin, Associated Press Sarah Rankin, Associated Press

Mikella Schuettler, Associated Press Mikella Schuettler, Associated Press

GRAHAM, N.C. (AP) — As he ran for sheriff in North Carolina against a longtime incumbent who had joined forces with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, Shannon Long found his campaign van was an obstacle with some voters.

The trust between law enforcement and Alamance County's growing Latino community was so fractured, Long said, that the vehicle emblazoned with "sheriff" made it a struggle to get some people to speak with him.

"They've been living in fear. They feel like they don't have a voice. They have been suppressed, oppressed; a lot of them are depressed. So they feel that they live in a community where they don't belong," Long, a pastor, business owner and former sheriff's deputy, told The Associated Press two weeks after defeating Republican Sheriff Terry Johnson in a campaign that some activists, voters and local officials say turned partly on questions about immigration enforcement and the treatment of Latino residents.

Johnson is one of a few sheriffs around the country who were ousted by challengers critical of their cooperation with President Donald Trump's push for mass deportations of people in the country illegally. While only a smattering, the results could spell trouble for other sheriffs who are seen as participants in Trump's crackdown and possibly hinder agreements that have become a cornerstone of the administration's efforts.

Johnson was among the first sheriffs to allow his deputies to enforce federal immigration laws under what's known as a 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Long, who ran as an independent, promised to curtail cooperation with ICE, which continues to rely on the cooperative pacts to boost arrest numbers despite a one-time infusion of $75 billion from Congress and hiring about 12,000 officers.

The administration has more than 2,700 such pacts with state and local agencies, up from 135 when Trump began his second term. The agreements, predominantly in the South, have deputized over 29,000 local law officers and resulted in more than 6,600 arrests in July, about 15% of all ICE arrests, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project that was analyzed by the advocacy group fwd.us.

national.title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
national.summary: Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were reportedly given 74 lashes in Qom.
national.body:
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.

Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.

Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.

This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.

In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.

At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.

On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.

national.title: U.S. to co-host 2031 Women's World Cup with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica
national.summary: The UK, led by England, will host the 2035 edition.
national.body:
Graham Dunbar, Associated Press Graham Dunbar, Associated Press

ZURICH (AP) — The United States will co-host another soccer World Cup in 2031, with the United Kingdom set to follow four years later.

FIFA on Monday confirmed the U.S. will co-host the 2031 Women's World Cup in a regional project together with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica. A UK-bid led by England was also ratified for the 2035 edition.

The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments and to reinvest all the profits in women's soccer. The 2031 edition will be expanded to feature 48 teams for the first time, in line with the men's World Cup.

"This will be the largest women's sporting event in history," the U.S. Soccer Federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, told FIFA members in a pre-vote presentation at the governing body's headquarters in Zurich. "Which means we have to deliver."

There were no rival bids for either tournament, ensuring that the U.S. and England — two of the heavyweights of women's soccer — will spearhead the hosting of the first expanded tournaments.

The U.S.-led 2031 project offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

The United Kingdom bid includes England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales and offers a choice from 19 venues, including Wembley Stadium in London.

national.title: The collapse of UN climate talks over fossil fuels was years in the making
national.summary: While negotiations collapsed over one main point of contention — whether to include language about fossil fuels, the main driver of global warming — this fight over this has been building for many years.
national.body:
Peter Prengaman, Associated Press Peter Prengaman, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — Going into this year's U.N. climate talks in Turkey, expectations were notably low. But the outcome on Sunday was even worse than expected — a failure to reach an overall agreement on fighting climate change at a time of frequent extreme weather events fueled by rising temperatures.

Gaining traction at this year's summit, known as COP31, was always going to be difficult. Leaders and everyday people alike have plenty to contend with in addition to extreme weather, from wars to shaky economies to fears about artificial intelligence. Last year's climate conference in Brazil, which had all the ingredients for an historic outcome, turned out to be a flop. And for the second year in a row, the United States, the world's richest country and historically No. 1 polluter, did not take part; the Trump administration has pulled the U.S. from climate negotiations.

Still, there was hope, among lifetime environmental campaigners, climate scientists and negotiators from many countries, that there would be some progress on confronting the main cause of climate change: coal, oil and gas.

The burning of these fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases, which go up into the atmosphere and raise global average temperatures, creating havoc on ecosystems and leading to more, and more intense, extreme weather events.

In simple terms, the solution is to burn less of these fuels over time and instead use sources of energy that don't release greenhouse gases, like solar, wind and geothermal. But there is nothing simple about getting countries to agree on a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, particularly major oil producers like Saudi Arabia, Russia and the United States, or major coal users like China and India.

So, even though fossil fuels are the cause of climate change, and the annual climate summits are convened to confront climate change, it's become all but impossible to have even the words "fossil fuels" show up in a final agreement, much less any detailed transition plan.

In the 30 years of climate negotiations, the one exception was the U.N. climate conference three years ago in Dubai, COP28, where the final decision encouraged countries to "transition away from fossil fuels." Fossil fuels were not mentioned in the final agreements in the following two conferences, and the current one, of course, had no final agreement.

national.title: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
national.summary: Interests of oil-producing countries, a US boycott and a dispute over finance may have torpedoed climate talks.
national.body:
Climate Editor Published 4 hours ago Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.

The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".

Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".

And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.

Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?

The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.

Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.

national.title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
national.summary: The impersonator, Canadian comedian Mark Critch, poked fun at the US president's search for a new press secretary and US-Canada trade talks.
national.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.

The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.

Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.

"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.

"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.

He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."

There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.

The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning.

The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.

national.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
national.summary: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.
national.body:
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the charity Oxfam says , external .

Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.

Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".

In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards".

Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".

Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

national.title: Medicare for All was once a long shot. Now universal healthcare is on the Democrats' agenda

WASHINGTON (AP) — What were once long-shot ideas around universal healthcare — championed by Sen. Bernie Sanders' Medicare for All — have suddenly been catapulted to the forefront of the Democratic agenda for the new Congress in January.

The party in its first 100 days is planning swift action on legislation to reverse recent Medicaid cuts that threaten to leave millions of people without care and to revive tax breaks that help people who buy insurance through the Affordable Care Act.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

But it's also becoming clear that the Democrats have far more ambitious healthcare goals as they prepare to take charge on Jan. 3, 2027.

Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, on track to become House speaker, announced his intentions to take steps toward Medicare for All in a post-midterm election speech that stunned health advocates. He listed proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age below 65, add dental, vision and hearing aid benefits, and open up healthcare to children as part of the incoming majority's plans — all aspects of Medicare for All.

Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, unveiled his push for portions of Medicare for All as he takes over the chairmanship of the Senate health committee.

And even former President Barack Obama encouraged newly elected Democrats to go beyond the ACA, also known as Obamacare, which was among his signature accomplishments in office.

"We got the ACA done, which was wonderful," Obama said, according to a transcript of his remarks to the incoming Democrats at the Capitol.

national.title: What Trump told PBS News about Jensen Huang before Nvidia reinstatement
national.summary: In a phone call with PBS News shortly after 8 a.m. EST Monday, Trump did not deny that he had been briefed, saying he was "not going to comment on anything having to do with that. You'll have to figure that out for yourself."
national.body:
President Donald Trump refused to say Monday whether he had been briefed on U.S. intelligence that the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been in contact with an official at China's top spy agency for more than a year around the same time period.

In a phone call with PBS News shortly after 8 a.m. EST Monday, Trump did not deny that he had been briefed, saying he was "not going to comment on anything having to do with that. You'll have to figure that out for yourself."

When asked for a second time about reporting from The New York Times that he had been briefed on the matter on at least two occasions, he said, "I don't want to comment on it now, I'm sorry. I won't comment on anything having to do with the story."

The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang, a Chinese woman who had a secret affair with Jensen Huang, had been in contact with a top official from the China Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 until the fall of this year.

The president also hinted that Jensen Huang, the embattled tech executive who has since admitted to multiple affairs with female employees, would be reinstated as the head of Nvidia.

"He's back where he should be, and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong from that standpoint." The president added that he thought Huang had "certainly learned a lesson."

Less than an hour later, the chip design behemoth announced that Huang had been reinstated as president and CEO , as well as a member of the board.

national.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
national.summary: The Nvidia chief executive has been at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom.
national.body:
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.

The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.

Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

national.summary: The debates could be play a key role in generating attention for what is expected to be a broad field of candidates vying to succeed Republican President Donald Trump.
national.body:
Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press

Democrats are planning a dozen presidential primary debates for what's expected to be a crowded field of 2028 candidates, with the first scheduled for June, the Democratic National Committee announced Monday.

The DNC's announcement comes before major candidates have launched campaigns to succeed term-limited Republican President Donald Trump and follows the party's convincing midterm performance , when Democrats flipped both the House and Senate and secured their biggest majority in the new Congress in decades.

DNC Chairman Ken Martin said in a statement the party is aimed at staying united and helping the eventual nominee win the White House.

"The DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle," he said in an emailed statement.

The debates could play a key role in generating attention for candidates and winnowing the field of possible nominees. Anticipating a large number of presidential hopefuls, the DNC said it will cap participation in each debate to 20 qualifying candidates over two nights, if needed.

The criteria for making the debate stage will be similar to 2020, when there was also a big field and a dozen debates, the DNC said, and will include meeting polling and other criteria such as grasroots fundraising.

More details are set to be announced in January, including specific times and locations for the debates, the DNC said, though the party determined five debates will be in 2027 and seven in 2028. The final primary debate is planned for March 2028.

national.title: The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
national.summary: Days after resigning while mired in scandal of extra-marital affairs, Nvidia's Jensen Huang is making a remarkable return.
national.body:
For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.

Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.

Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.

So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?

Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.

The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.

Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

There was an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base in the early morning, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia, local authorities said.

Zelensky added that Ukraine's attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.

The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.

Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

Libya's two governments - the UN-recognised government in the capital, Tripoli, and a rival administration in the east - have both condemned the attack.

The Tripoli foreign ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the conflict.

It said foreign forces would not be allowed to use Libyan ports and civilian infrastructure for military purposes.

national.title: More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from Don Toliver concert after an unknown substance sickens fans
national.summary: One person was hospitalized, and more than 50 were assessed for eye and respiratory symptoms.
national.body:
Jill Lawless, Associated Press Jill Lawless, Associated Press

LONDON (AP) — More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from a concert by American rapper Don Toliver and over 80 were treated by medics after an unknown irritant was released in the crowd, authorities in the English city of Manchester said Monday.

Greater Manchester Police said officers were called around 10 p.m. (2200 GMT) Sunday to the Co-op Live arena after reports of people being affected by a substance, initially believed to be tear gas. Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue.

The force declared a "major incident," which allows different emergency services to coordinate their response.

Concertgoer Ben Stevenson told the Manchester Evening News he was in the standing area of the arena when he "started coughing and (my) eyes were kind of itchy."

He said Toliver left the stage and the venue lights came on, but it was not until almost an hour later that an announcement said, "due to an unforeseen issue, the show is over, and please make your way out at your own pace."

Joey Howe, a concertgoer, told BBC Radio Manchester that there was a "horrible smell" and people rushed out of the venue.

"People were coming through in wheelchairs, choking. It was really distressing," he said.

national.title: Prominent Zimbabwean preacher arrested on sexual assault allegations
national.summary: Uebert Angel, a British-Zimbabwean national, leads a charismatic church with branches in several countries.
national.body:
A well-known Zimbabwean preacher has been arrested on indecent assault and sodomy allegations, local police said.

Uebert Angel, who leads an international charismatic church with branches around the world, was arrested during a church service in Harare on Sunday. Pictures and footage of the dramatic arrest have since been circulated online.

In one video, a convoy of vehicles is seen escorting the self-styled prophet as he sits in the back of a police van surrounded by armed police officers.

The controversial founder of Spirit Embassy was also appointed Zimbabwe's special presidential envoy and ambassador-at-large to Europe and the Americas back in 2021 by President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

In 2023, he made headlines when an undercover report by Al Jazeera claimed that he had offered to use his diplomatic status to launder large amounts of money through a gold-smuggling scheme in the country.

According to the Qatar-based network, Angel, 48, told reporters working undercover that the scheme was approved by President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Zimbabwean police only released a brief statement confirming his arrest but a member of his team told reporters the British Zimbabwean national was still in police custody and it was unclear when he'd make an appearance in court.

"It can be in the afternoon or tomorrow [Tuesday]. We are still within the legal framework [for him to appear in court]," Professor Lovemore Madhuku told state-owned broadcaster ZBC in a clip posted online.

national.title: Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
national.summary: Eight suspects are arrested after firing on soldiers trying to re-establish order following the arrest of 'El Chapo Isidro'.
national.body:
Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.

The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.

Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.

The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.

In a statement published on social media , external , the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age.

It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.

The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.

It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".

national.title: Nigeria's president says he is also hit by water and power cuts plaguing country
national.summary: Bola Tinubu says he was shaving last week when the water cut out - an experience familiar to many Nigerians.
national.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.

He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.

He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.

Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.

He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].

"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.

Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.

Last year, 10bn naira (£5.5m; $7.2m), was allocated in the budget for the installation of a solar mini-grid in the Aso Villa as part of efforts to address rising electricity bills and unstable power supply.

national.body:

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that maritime drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.

Ukrainian forces deployed seven drones in the operation that struck the Russian navy corvette in the Mediterranean, according to Zelenskyy. The ship, the Merkury, was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbor, he said in a post on X.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to comment on the attack, saying that Russia's Defense Ministry would provide more information "if deemed to be appropriate."

The operation, conducted some 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

Ukraine has at times embarrassed Moscow during the war with attacks such as Operation Spiderweb in June 2025, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft parked at air bases across Russia. national.summary: Trump, who has a close personal relationship with Huang, called for the reinstatement as recently as Sunday night and took credit for the board's decision in an interview Monday with CNBC.
national.body:

In a surprise move, Nvidia's board on Monday reinstated CEO Jensen Huang, apparently at the behest of President Donald Trump, just days after rejecting Huang's offer to return to the chipmaker where he was a leading evangelist for artificial intelligence.

The sudden reversal was the latest twist in the fallout from Huang's admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board Chairman Harvey C. Jones said in a statement.

Trump, who has a close personal relationship with Huang, called for the reinstatement as recently as Sunday night and took credit for the board's decision in an interview Monday with CNBC.

The president said he spoke to Huang about the reinstatement Sunday, and the CEO assured him that he would work harder than before his fall. Trump also said his administration assured Nvidia that there were no national security concerns about Huang's return.

"The board decided to do what we wanted them to do," the president said.

local.title: This flu season is already way ahead of last year's pace
local.summary: With the holidays quickly approaching, health officials are urging people to get vaccinated.
local.body:
Flu season is already off to a fast and aggressive start both statewide and in Greater Rochester.

As of Nov. 14, Monroe County has reported 1,259 confirmed cases of influenza, more than six times the number of cases that were reported last year at this time.

There are also 129 flu-related hospitalizations and fewer than 10 flu-related deaths. State and county data trackers do not provide an exact number of deaths until the number exceeds 10.

In a virtual news conference Monday afternoon, Monroe County Commissioner of Public Health Dr. Marielena Vélez de Brown stressed the importance of vaccination.

"The vaccine may not prevent every infection, but it can certainly reduce your chances of getting very sick and lower your risk of ending up in the hospital," she said.

Monroe County's current flu vaccination rate is 26.5%, higher than the statewide rate of 22%.

The flu vaccine is recommended to everyone beginning at 6 months of age.

"With the holidays approaching, many of us will be traveling, gathering indoors, and spending time with family and friends," Vélez de Brown said. "So, getting vaccinated isn't just about protecting your own health; it's also about protecting the people you're gathering with."

local.title: Rochester firefighters extinguish massive blaze at the former Hawkeye plant
local.summary: Rochester firefighters arrived to find heavy smoke and flames on the third floor of the sprawling former camera manufacturing complex.
local.body:
The former Kodak Hawkeye building on St. Paul Street became the scene of a massive fire Sunday night.

Rochester firefighters arrived to find heavy smoke and flames on the third floor of the sprawling former camera manufacturing complex.

Lt. Howard Villegas of the Rochester Fire Department said large amounts of stored materials helped fuel the blaze and made it difficult to extinguish.

“There was a lot of cardboard, and cardboard boxes filled with several items," Villegas said.

A firefighter was taken to the hospital for observation and is expected to make a full recovery with no significant injuries.

Villegas also stated, “it seemed that any occupants may have exited the structure prior to our arrival, but this was what was witnessed by bystanders.”

Crews advanced multiple hose lines, ventilated the building, and worked to stop the fire from spreading. Despite challenging conditions inside the multi-story building, crews were able to keep most of the damage confined to the third floor, according to the department.

local.body:
Empire State Development on Monday announced the completion of Ultrapak, LLC's expansion and modernization project at its long-term facility in the city of Dunkirk.

Supported by up to $120,000 in performance-based Excelsior Jobs Program tax credits, the completed $800,000 project integrates advanced equipment to increase domestic production and reduce reliance on offshore manufacturing. As a result of this infrastructure expansion, Ultrapak has committed to creating 10 new skilled jobs in Western New York as manufacturing output increases.

"Under Gov. (Kathy) Hochul's leadership, New York State continues to strengthen its position as a global manufacturing powerhouse," said Empire State Development President, CEO & Commissioner Hope Knight. "The completion of Ultrapak's expansion in Dunkirk is a direct result of her commitment to investing in the high-tech equipment and infrastructure local businesses need to scale. Alongside major regional anchors like Cummins Jamestown Engine Plant and Wells Enterprises, this project is fueling sustained economic growth and supporting a dedicated workforce in Western New York."

Since 1987, Ultrapak has been manufacturing heat-shrinkable sleeves which are used as decorative labels, tamper-evidence protection and unitizing sleeves. These sleeves largely serve the food and beverage, cosmetics, and pharmaceutical industries.

Khalid Khan, Founder and CEO of Ultrapak said, "By bringing this advanced production capacity directly to Chautauqua County, we are answering the call for stronger domestic supply chains. The successful installation of our printing press allows us to drastically reduce long lead times and vulnerabilities associated with offshore manufacturing. We are incredibly grateful to Empire State Development and our local partners for helping us scale our operations. This investment ensures that our customers nationwide can source premium, American-made flexible packaging with unparalleled speed, reliability, and precision."

Located at 134 Franklin Ave., Ultrapak has a long-trusted history serving national accounts, ranging from startups to established brands. Beyond shrink sleeves, Ultrapak also serves the flexible packaging market with flexible pouches and with sleeve application services.

"Chautauqua County has a proud manufacturing history, and investments like Ultrapak's demonstrate that our manufacturing sector continues to evolve and thrive,” Chautauqua County Executive PJ Wendel said. “This expansion represents a commitment to our local workforce, the creation of new job opportunities, and the long-term economic vitality of our communities. We are grateful to Ultrapak for its continued confidence in Chautauqua County and to our state and local partners for helping make this project possible."

local.body:
Two people have been taken to UPMC Hospital in Pittsburgh after their Mina French Creek Road home exploded on Sunday.

Sherman volunteer firefighters and several mutual aid fire departments responded to 2170 Mina French Creek Road, Mina, at 6:05 p.m. Sunday for a reported explosion and structure fire. After extinguishing the fire, the Chautauqua County Fire Investigation Team was requested to the scene to conduct an origin and cause fire investigation. The investigation found that there was a propane gas leak in the home which was ignited by an undetermined source in the basement of the structure which resulted in an explosion and structure fire.

As a result of the incident, two adult victims were transported to UPMC in Pittsburgh for life threatening injuries. The fire is being ruled as accidental in nature and the structure was a complete loss.

local.title: Declining enrollment helped prompt C/S/P merger talks
local.summary: December 15 marks the official voting day that eligible residents in the Clymer, Sherman and Panama school districts will be deciding whether or not to move forward and merge the three school districts into one. A feasibility study that has been done on the potential merger includes the details behi
local.body:
December 15 marks the official voting day that eligible residents in the Clymer, Sherman and Panama school districts will be deciding whether or not to move forward and merge the three school districts into one.

A feasibility study that has been done on the potential merger includes the details behind the decision to look into this merger, including why the three communities are considering a change and how this change could affect the students in these three districts. One of the most major reasons behind looking into this merger is the decline in enrollment in all three districts.

CSP Merger Study Project Coordinator, Shelly O'Boyle, shared that over the last 30 years student enrollment across the three districts has dropped by 52 percent, as outlined in the merger feasibility study. This percentage means that enrollment across all three districts has fallen from 2,169 students in 1995 to 1,041 in 2025. Today, Clymer, Panama and Sherman have three of the five smallest student populations out of all 18 school districts in Chautauqua County.

The feasibility study projects that with a combined district there will be between 920 and 980 students total by 2030. As individual grades shrink, O'Boyle said that some classes are projected to have fewer than 15 students and it becomes much harder for each district to afford specialized teachers, classes and buildings on their own.

"While shrinking enrollment is one of the main reasons for exploring a merger, the study shows that combining resources could create new opportunities for students, which local residents ranked as their top priority," O'Boyle said. "All three districts already have strong graduation rates. Merging at the high school level would allow students to share a combined 60 electives and 29 college-level courses through Jamestown Community College and Hilbert College without small class sizes getting in the way."

Outside the classroom, the three districts have already successfully shared multiple CSP sports teams. O'Boyle said a formal merger is set to make those teams more sustainable, open the door to new sports, and bring together 21 clubs, music and arts programs.

"For special education, the study recommends that a merged district would form a new committee made up of staff from all three communities," O'Boyle said. "This approach would keep student support familiar while offering more special education services in-house."

local.body:
On Nov. 10, Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders released a new book entitled, “Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy.”

Unlike most midterm Republican candidates, Sanders won reelection in a landslide.

I had the opportunity to hear her speak about her new book at the Nixon Library on Veterans Day and was so inspired that I, like others in the room, wondered out loud if she should be on the GOP short list for presidential nominee in 2028.

Her newest book, “Unapologetic,” tracks her journey serving as press secretary in the White House to becoming the first woman elected governor of Arkansas. It gets really personal as she shares the fear she overcame in her battle with cancer that was diagnosed just 60 days before her first election — and the faith that sustained her then and continues to guide her every day.

As she first ran for governor, Sanders addressed issues that she believes matter most to Arkansans: education, lower taxes, jobs and public safety. And she delivered as a conservative on those issues and was unapologetically pro-life.

Sanders was reelected by a 15-point margin in an election cycle where Republicans suffered crushing losses all across America, including in her neighboring state of Texas.

Every Republican state official on the ballot was elected, along with the entire Arkansas Republican congressional delegation.

While she has supported many of President Donald Trump’s policy positions, Sarah expresses a nuanced view on the issue of artificial intelligence. She supports guardrails around AI and opposed a provision in the original version of the One Big Beautiful Bill that would have prevented states from regulating AI. That provision was stripped following objections by her and only a handful of other Republicans.

local.title: The OBSERVER’s View: Safety net spending problem has many causes
local.summary: The Chautauqua County Legislature doesn’t have much choice but to pay the ever-escalating bill for safety net spending – but that doesn’t mean the county has to handle this expense the same way it has over the past few years, either. In October county lawmakers approved a resolution that moves $2,13
local.body:
The Chautauqua County Legislature doesn’t have much choice but to pay the ever-escalating bill for safety net spending - but that doesn’t mean the county has to handle this expense the same way it has over the past few years, either.

In October county lawmakers approved a resolution that moves $2,130,000 from its unassigned fund balance to the Safety Net account to pay the county’s share of costs for single adults; childless couples; children living with a caretaker other than a parent; families of persons abusing drugs or alcohol; families of persons refusing drug alcohol screening, assessment, or treatment; people who have exceeded the 60-month limit on assistance; and non-citizens who are eligible for temporary assistance, but who are not eligible for federal reimbursement. The good news is that the $2.13 million is less than the $2.8 million the county Department of Social Services had requested earlier in the year to cover the shortfall. The bad news is that the drop county officials saw in June that prompted the earlier request to be rescinded wasn’t sustainable.

In fact, if there’s one thing the county can take to the bank next year, it’s that safety net spending will exceed what the county has budgeted. We’d still like to see the safety net budget increased in the budget each year so that mid-year adjustments aren’t needed. In our opinion, that number is at least $16 million in 2027, if not closer to $16.5 million. Doing so would mean county residents have a more clear understanding how much safety net programs are costing each year and avoids the mid-year budget adjustment.

It’s nice to have the surplus to make up the difference between budget spending for safety net program costs and what is actually spent, but it is preferable to actually set the budget high enough that the yearly budget adjustment isn’t needed.

Just as importantly, we aren’t sure why the county didn’t just allocate more money this summer. We hope it’s not to avoid Legislator Fred Johnson’s push to reduce other departments’ budgets to pay for safety net program spending needs. We agree with Johnson, finding the money in the approved budget is preferable to simply taking from the county surplus. But it is a lot more work for county department heads, and given the slight difference between the June and October DSS spending requests, we wonder if the delay in appropriating the money was to make the increased spending take place later in the year so Johnson and those who agree with his line of thinking would have no choice but to use the surplus to pay the increased cost.

local.title: Cassadaga Valley eyes $18.2M capital project
local.summary: SINCLAIRVILLE — A proposed $18.2 million capital improvement project at Cassadaga Valley Central School is set to have no additional tax impact for members of the school district. local.body:
SINCLAIRVILLE -- A proposed $18.2 million capital improvement project at Cassadaga Valley Central School is set to have no additional tax impact for members of the school district.

This planned project has been in the works for a while, with planning beginning in the 2024-2025 school year. Superintendent Tammy Mangus noted that caring for the district's schools is ongoing work and that the district has a long history of using the Building Conditions Survey, mandated for every five years, to identify the buildings' core needs. This is followed by the creation of capital outlays and capital improvement projects to ensure that the district's buildings maintain their "breathtaking beauty while evaluating and addressing building condition needs and student needs."

"This proposal brings those pieces together: taking care of aging facilities, improving spaces for students, and planning the financial commitment so we can sustain it," Mangus said. "The proposed $18.2 million project addresses needs at Sinclairville Elementary School, the Middle-High School, and our Bus Garage."

The project at Sinclairville Elementary includes replacing outdated classroom heating and ventilation equipment, adding cafeteria cooling, upgrading the water distribution systems, replacing deteriorated flooring and addressing the kitchen cooler and related structural needs. At the Middle-High School, the work includes heating and cooling improvements, including cooling for the gym and third floor; water distribution upgrades; classroom flooring; and improvements to the Cougar Café and cafeteria. It also includes converting the middle school locker rooms into student service suites and an updated health office. At the Bus Garage, the proposal includes heating and ventilation improvements in the bus bays and roof replacement.

"If voters approve the project in December, the anticipated schedule includes design in 2027, New York State Education Department review in 2028, and construction from approximately 2029 through 2031," Mangus said. "That timeline also helps explain why planning ahead matters. These projects take time to move from identifying a need to completing the work."

Mangus said this capital improvement project is important because education provides students with opportunities, and the places where students learn need to be able to support those opportunities on a daily basis. This means having dependable heat, appropriate ventilation, functioning water systems, sound roofs, and spaces where students can receive the care and support they need.

local.body:
While the Chautauqua County Industrial Development Agency is still working on getting 65 acres ready for development, they're moving ahead, doubling the size of the project.

For the last few years the county IDA has been trying to create a "shovel-ready" site in Ripley near I-90. The belief is that once this land is ready, developers would be willing to start a new company or relocate an existing one to the area.

The IDA is in the process of putting in necessary sewer, water, gas and electric to the site. They've also addressed the zoning and done the necessary environmental studies.

IDA Chief Executive Officer Mark Geise has said previously that he regularly gets calls from developers that are looking for large plots of land that are ready to be developed.

Because of this, county leaders have been looking to get land ready so a large company or industry could come to the area.

During the November IDA meeting, the IDA's Board of Directors approved purchasing 85 acres of land for $2,208,180. The property is currently owned by Cochrane Farms, Inc.

Geise said at the meeting they are purchasing the property for around $26,000 an acre, which is what it’s appraised at.

Most of the money has been coming from various state and federal grants.

Tom Jackson, a fiery cornerstone of the Orange Crush defense with the Denver Broncos who went on to even more fame as a beloved broadcaster on ESPN, has died, his family and the network announced Sunday. He was 75.

Jackson’s family informed ESPN that he died Friday, but it was their wishes that his death not be announced until the start of the network’s “Sunday NFL Countdown” show by Jackson’s longtime friend and on-air partner Chris Berman. A cause of death was not given.

“Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst. There was nobody kinder, more thoughtful, more loyal or more engaging than him. And when it came to laughter, Tom’s was frequent and unmistakable,” Berman said. “Tom was my best friend professionally and personally. If you ever met him or just knew him from watching ESPN, he was your best friend, too.”

Berman said Jackson made a surprise visit a couple of weeks ago to ESPN, where he worked for 32 years over two stints after playing 14 seasons for the Broncos, and that the two talked on Tuesday.

A fourth-round draft pick out of Louisville in 1973, Jackson was an inspirational leader of Denver’s first Super Bowl team in 1977. He started 177 games for the Broncos between 1973-86, retiring after the team’s second Super Bowl appearance. He was a first-team All-Pro in 1977 and a second-team All-Pro the following season; he also was a three-time Pro Bowler.

The Broncos held a moment of silence and showed a video tribute to Jackson prior to their game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.

Following his playing days, Jackson had a second career at ESPN from 1987-2016 and was featured on “Sunday NFL Countdown” and “NFL Primetime.”

Before the internet, and before NBC took over the Sunday night package in 2006, “NFL Primetime” was must-see viewing for fans and players because it showed highlights from all the games, as well as the interaction between Berman and Jackson, who often finished each other’s sentences.
